story.title: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal for AI chips, Elon Musk says - CNBC

facts.text: (Bloomberg) -- Elon Musk said SpaceX ( SPCX ) has closed a $40 billion debt deal to pay for the chips it needs to fuel its artificial intelligence ambitions.
With the latest structure, SpaceX would avoid a repeat of a financing attempt last year by Musk's AI startup, xAI.
In that deal, an entity sought as much as $20 billion of off-balance sheet debt through a sale-leaseback agreement with Valor Equity Partners.
SpaceX hasn't been completely immune to growing concerns over the AI infrastructure boom.
In noting SpaceX's diversified business, Musk sought to differentiate the company from so-called neoclouds that sell high-end computing power to technology companies.
"As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," Musk said in his post.
Some will make it through, but not many." He later said that SpaceX won't buy any neoclouds, calling it "pointless."
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
It wasn't immediately clear from Musk's post on Sunday what he meant by the deal being "closed" or whether investors had agreed to pricing for the debt.
Elon Musk said SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power artificial intelligence systems.
The proposed financing would use a special purpose vehicle to keep the debt off SpaceX's balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit ratings, according to Bloomberg.

The financing underscores the enormous capital requirements of the AI boom, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models.
Musk also said that debt markets have largely shut off access to financing for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers.

Elon Musk announced on Sunday that SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase graphics processing units (GPUs), marking another major investment in artificial intelligence as technology companies race to expand their computing infrastructure.
The expansion also comes with substantial spending commitments.
Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen expects fourth-quarter capital expenditure to reach between $35 billion and $40 billion.
Musk also recently told investors that merging SpaceX and Tesla would be “a good idea”, citing increasing technological overlap between the two companies.

The developments highlight Musk's broader push into AI computing and semiconductor manufacturing, even as rising infrastructure costs and tightening financing conditions raise questions about the sustainability of the industry's rapid expansion.

While outlining SpaceX's financing plans, Musk warned that companies relying heavily on AI infrastructure revenue could face mounting financial pressure.
He said debt markets "have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers."
The financing comes as artificial intelligence takes on a larger role in SpaceX's business.
The company's revenue surged 161% year-on-year to $14.58 billion in the quarter ended September 30, while AI revenue jumped nearly tenfold to $7.56 billion.
Musk predicted consolidation and potential failures among neocloud operators, which provide specialised computing infrastructure for AI workloads.
Musk also ruled out SpaceX acquiring neocloud businesses, describing such a move as “pointless.”
The project aims to produce its first test chip around May or June 2027, with large-scale production targeted for the third quarter of 2028.
In a post on X, Musk attributed the successful fundraising to SpaceX's investment-grade status and its established revenue streams from Starlink satellite internet services and rocket launches.
SpaceX has secured $40 billion in debt financing to buy graphics processing units (GPUs), the chips used to run AI systems, Elon Musk said in a post on X on Sunday.
According to Musk, most of the debt is callable, meaning SpaceX can repay it early.
In a second post, he said the money would cover chips arriving in the first and second quarters of next year and would not significantly affect spending this quarter.
SpaceX closed $40B of debt for GPUs, but we’re investment grade and have Starlink & launch revenue.
Musk did not name the lenders or disclose the interest rate, and SpaceX has not published the financing terms.
He predicted that many of the more than 200 neocloud companies would fail or merge, naming neither specific targets nor a timeframe.
Musk added that SpaceX would not acquire any of them.
Musk credited SpaceX’s investment-grade credit rating and revenue from Starlink and rocket launches with helping it secure the financing.
SpaceX absorbed Musk’s AI company xAI and went public in June.
Last week, SpaceX reported that revenue rose 161% to $14.58 billion in the quarter ending September 30.
AI revenue grew almost tenfold to $7.56 billion over the same period.
On the same earnings call, chief financial officer Bret Johnsen said SpaceX expects to spend between $35 billion and $40 billion on equipment and facilities in the current quarter.
The proposed deal would combine approximately $10 billion in bank loans with $30 billion in investment-grade debt.
“Debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money” for companies without substantial revenue streams outside AI data centres, Musk wrote.
SpaceX’s chief executive also predicted a shakeout among neoclouds, the firms that rent out AI computing power.
